HFRS bivalent inactivated vaccine (HFRSbiv) with Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) strains isolated 20 years ago have been used in key HFRS endemic provinces in China for HFRS prevention. After decades of effective implementation of comprehensive prevention and control measures, HFRS has entered a stage of epidemic fluctuation at low-level in China. However, the continuous transmission of the virus among rodent host animals may lead to dynamic changes in genetic diversity and immunogenicity of the virus, which may affect the pathogenic mechanism of the virus and the protective effect of vaccines. It is necessary to carry out timely monitoring and evaluation of the immunogenicity of HV. METHODOLOGY/PRINCIPAL FINDINGS: A panel of sera was established by screening serum samples from HFRS patients at convalescent phase and individuals who had received standardized immunization with HFRSbiv. Neutralizing antibody titers against HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi, SEOV vaccine strain L99, and three representative epidemic strains from different genotypes (HTNV: SX26, SEOV: LN03 and FJ-17) were measured using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay-based microneutralization test (MN-ELISA). HV-neutralizing antibodies were detected from all the selected serum samples. Among HFRS patients, 47.92% (23/48) were identified as HTNV infection, 27.08% (13/48) were with SEOV infection, and 25% (12/48) were untypable. There is a significant difference in the titers of neutralizing antibodies against vaccine strains and epidemic strains detected in the serum samples. For HTNV, both patient and vaccinee sera exhibited significantly higher geometric mean titer (GMT) against vaccine strain 84FLi than against epidemic strain SX26 (1:386.08 vs. 1:223.04, P < 0.001; 1:137.94 vs. 1:110.37, P < 0.05, respectively). For SEOV, patient sera showed significantly lower GMT against vaccine strain L99 than against epidemic strain LN03 (1:177.02 vs. 1:297.71, P < 0.01), and vaccinee sera showed significantly lower GMT against L99 than against epidemic strain FJ-17 (1:97.52 vs. 1:243.71, P < 0.001). Significant immunogenicity heterogeneity was observed between SEOV epidemic strains LN03 and FJ-17. CONCLUSIONS/SIGNIFICANCE: The genetic diversity and immunogenicity of HV, which causes HFRS, have certain geographical regional characteristics. The levels of cross neutralizing antibodies induced by infection of HV from different genotypes may vary significantly, but still provide sufficient cross protection. The HFRSbiv currently used in China could induce broad neutralizing antibody, the cross-protective efficacy might vary against different circulating strains and genotypes. It is of great significance to strengthen the monitoring of genetic characteristics of regional specific circulating viral strains, regularly evaluate the matching degree between vaccine protection effectiveness and epidemic strains, predict and evaluate the transmission and pathogenic risks of HV, and timely optimize HFRS prevention and control strategies and measures.

Author summary Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by HV remains a serious threat to global public health security, with its epidemic scope continuing to expand. After more than 20 years of application in China, HFRS bivalent inactivated vaccine (HFRSbiv) has been proven to effectively prevent HFRS. However, the evolution and mutation of the virus pose challenges to this specific prevention and control measure. In this study, the levels of neutralizing antibodies against the vaccine strains and the current circulating virus strains in the panel of sera collected from confirmed HFRS patients at convalescent phase and adults who had received standardized immunization with HFRSbiv were evaluated. There are significant differences in the immunogenicity of cross protection induced by locally prevalent HV strains and vaccine strains (HTNV 84FLi and SEOV L99), which suggested that the effectiveness of HFRSbiv may vary in different parts of China. Our findings highlight the importance of the monitoring of genetic characteristics and immunogenicity of regional specific circulating viral strains to predict and evaluate the transmission and pathogenic risks for timely optimization of HFRS prevention and control strategies and measures. Introduction Several rodent-borne hantaviruses are recognized as important human pathogens causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) primarily in Asia and Europe, and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas, which are mainly acquired through the inhalation of infectious respiratory particles from rodent urine or feces. The viruses are distributed globally, and approximately 200,000 cases are reported annually, posing a persistent threat to human health [1]. In China, Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are the causative agents of HFRS, and the infection has a relatively wide distribution, with the highest annual reported cases exceeding 110000 in 1980s [2]. Although the annual incidence of HFRS had significantly decreased and maintained a low level in the last two decades, the geographical distribution range of Hantavirus (HV) infection had shown an expanding trend, and the virus presents a more abundant genetic diversity [3]. HV are predominantly hosted by rodents and exhibit strict host specificity, each hantavirus species is primarily carried and transmitted by one or several closely related reservoir hosts [4]. Virus–host adaptive evolution is influenced by ecological environments, host switching events, and gene selection pressures, contributing to the genetic diversity of hantaviruses. Moreover, as segmented RNA viruses, HV possess the capacity for genetic reassortment, enabling the exchange of genomic segments between two parental viruses co-infecting the same cell, thereby generating progeny viruses genetically distinct from both parents [5]. The frequency of segment exchange and the co-infection rate within the same host cell affect the success of genomic reassortment [6]. With the rapid development of laboratory testing technology and the expansion of pathogen monitoring scope, new HV strains continued to be discovered, presenting rich genetic diversity with regional characteristics in China [3,7]. It has been demonstrated that immunization with HFRS bivalent inactivated vaccine (HFRSbiv) which contains HTNV and SEOV, was an effective measure for HFRS prevention. HFRSbiv targeting HTNV and SEOV had been licensed for over two decades. Combined with comprehensive interventions such as immunization, rodent control and environmental sanitation, the disease burden of HFRS in China has been significantly reduced [8,9]. However, the vaccine strains used in China (e.g., HTNV PS-6, SD9805, and SEOV L99, HB9908) were isolated more than 20 years ago. Antigenic variation may exist among different strains within the same serotype, and its impact on vaccine protective efficacy remains unclear. Therefore, evaluating the immunogenicity of regional epidemic HV strains, as well as the immunogenic matching and cross-protection between vaccine strains and currently circulating strains, is practically important. In this study, a serum panel was established using serum samples collected from confirmed HFRS patients and HFRS vaccinees for a comparative analysis of the immunogenicity of HV circulating in China and vaccine strains using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay-based microneutralization test (MN-ELISA). The neutralizing antibody levels against vaccine strains and representative epidemic strains were systematically compared to elucidate immunogenicity differences and to provide experimental evidence for the scientific evaluation of the protective efficacy of HFRS vaccine. Materials and methods Ethics statement This study received ethics approval from the Ethical Committee of National Institute for Viral Disease Control and Prevention, Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Study subjects A total of 48 convalescent serum samples from HFRS patients and 28 serum samples from individuals who had completed a three-dose regimen with HFRSbiv were collected between 2019 and 2020 from Heilongjiang Province, which belonged to HFRS national surveillance system. The median interval between disease onset and serum collection for HFRS patients was 14 days, with an interquartile range (IQR) of 10.5 to 19.5 days. Serum samples from vaccinees were collected within one month after the third (booster) dose. HV amplification and titration The HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi, SEOV vaccine strain L99, and previously isolated epidemic strains SX26, LN03, and FJ-17 from HFRS national surveillance system were selected for neutralization assays. All strains were propagated in Vero-E6 cells prior to use. Viral replication was confirmed by quantitative real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) and indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA). Viral titers were determined by plaque assay. Virus resuscitation, propagation, and identification. HV vaccine strains (84FLi, L99) and epidemic strains (SX26, LN03, FJ-17) were thawed on ice and used to infect Vero-E6 cells. Culture supernatants were collected on day 7 post-infection for HV nucleic acid detection by qRT-PCR. Concurrently, cell antigen slides were prepared for IFA. Plaque assay for viral titration. Vero-E6 cells cultured for 24 h were seeded into 6-well plates and incubated overnight at 37°C with 5% CO2. After forming confluent monolayer, the monolayers were washed, and 500 μL of MEM maintenance medium was added to each well. Serial 10-fold dilutions (10−1 to 10−5) of virus stocks were prepared in MEM, and 500 μL of each dilution was inoculated per well in duplicate. Plates were incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2 for 1.5–2 h for adsorption. After removal of the inoculum, 3 mL of pre-warmed (42°C) agarose overlay (mainly 2 x MEM containing 10% fetal bovine serum,2% Gibco HEPES,1% Penicillin-Streptomycin and 2% low-melting-point agarose) was added per well. Once solidified, plates were inverted and incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2. Seven days later, a second agarose overlay, which was identical to that of the first overlay, with the addition of 3% neutral red to facilitate plaque visualization, was added, and incubation continued for an additional 48–72 h. Plaques were observed and counted. Viral titers were calculated as plaque-forming units per milliliter (PFU/mL): PFU/mL = (average plaque count at a given dilution × reciprocal of dilution) / virus inoculum volume (mL/well). Detection of serum HV IgG antibodies HV IgG antibodies in all serum samples were detected using a commercial HV IgG antibody ELISA kit (Beijing Beier Bioengineering Co., Ltd., enzyme immunoassay). Positive and negative controls were included. All procedures and result interpretation were performed strictly in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Neutralizing antibody assay (MN-ELISA) A fixed-virus (100 PFU/0.1 mL) microneutralization assay was employed. Sera were heat-inactivated at 56°C and serially diluted 2-fold in 96-well plates (starting dilution 1:10 for vaccinees and 1:20 for patients, ending at 1:10240), with three replicates per dilution. Each virus strain (84FLi, L99, SX26, LN03, FJ-17) was diluted to working concentration, and 50 μL of virus was mixed with an equal volume of diluted serum. The mixtures were incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2 for 1 h. Subsequently, 100 μL of Vero-E6 cell suspension was added to each well. Virus-positive and cell-negative controls were included. After seven days of incubation at 37°C, 5% CO2, supernatants were discarded, and cells were fixed with cold acetone and inactivated under UV light. After washing, 100 μL of detection antibody mixture (HV monoclonal antibody L13F3 at 1:3200 dilution and HRP-conjugated rabbit anti-mouse IgG at 1:1000 dilution, pre-mixed) was added per well and incubated at 37°C for 45 min. After washing, 100 μL of the mixed TMB substrate solution was added to each well and incubated for 10 min at room temperature in the dark. The reaction was stopped by adding 50 μL of 2 M H2SO4 per well, and the optical density (OD) was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader. Determination of neutralizing antibody titer and virus typing The neutralizing antibody titer was defined as the highest serum dilution that inhibited 50% of viral infection. The cutoff value (X) for positivity was calculated as: X = [(mean OD of cell-positive controls – mean OD of cell-negative controls)/2) + mean OD of cell-negative controls [10]. Samples with OD values below X were considered positive for neutralization, and the reciprocal of the highest dilution showing positivity was taken as the neutralizing antibody titer. For virus typing, the neutralizing antibody titers against the HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi and the SEOV vaccine strain L99 were compared. If the titer against one type was ≥ 4-fold higher than that against the other, the infection was assigned to that type; otherwise, it was considered untypable. Statistical analysis Raw data were entered, organized, and analyzed using Excel 2019 and GraphPad Prism 10.1.2. Neutralizing antibody titers were expressed as geometric mean titer (GMT). Comparisons among multiple groups were performed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). For non-normally distributed data, non-parametric tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank test for two-group comparisons, Friedman test for paired multiple-group comparisons) were applied. A P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results HV amplification and titer determination To obtain working virus stocks for subsequent neutralization assays, five HV strains (vaccine strains: 84FLi, L99; epidemic strains: SX26, LN03, FJ-17) were resuscitated, propagated, and titrated. All strains replicated efficiently in Vero-E6 cells. On day 7 post-infection, culture supernatants were collected and tested by qRT-PCR, all yielding positive results. IFA revealed typical bright green specific fluorescent granules in infected cells, which were absent in negative control cells, confirming intact viral infectivity (Fig 1). Viral titers were determined by plaque assay. All strains formed classical plaques at a 10−3 dilution (Fig 2). The calculated viral titers (PFU/mL) were as follows: 84FLi, 3.08 × 106; L99, 2.25 × 106; SX26, 5.13 × 105; LN03, 1.23 × 104; FJ-17, 1.65 × 106. These results confirmed successful amplification of all strains for subsequent neutralization assays. Note: The observations were performed at ×200 magnification. (A) 84FLi; (B) L99; (C) SX26; (D) LN03; (E) FJ-17; (F) Negative control cells. Note: plaque assays were performed in 6-well plates (well diameter: 35 mm). (A) 84FLi; (B) L99; (C) SX26; (D) LN03; (E) FJ-17; (F) Negative control. Demographic characteristics and HV typing of HFRS patients Among the 48 HFRS patients, 38 were male and 10 were female, with a median age of 53 years. full_text_sections.full_text: Figures Abstract Background Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantavirus (HV) remains a significant public health burden in the world. HFRS bivalent inactivated vaccine (HFRSbiv) with Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) strains isolated 20 years ago have been used in key HFRS endemic provinces in China for HFRS prevention. After decades of effective implementation of comprehensive prevention and control measures, HFRS has entered a stage of epidemic fluctuation at low-level in China. However, the continuous transmission of the virus among rodent host animals may lead to dynamic changes in genetic diversity and immunogenicity of the virus, which may affect the pathogenic mechanism of the virus and the protective effect of vaccines. It is necessary to carry out timely monitoring and evaluation of the immunogenicity of HV. Methodology/principal findings A panel of sera was established by screening serum samples from HFRS patients at convalescent phase and individuals who had received standardized immunization with HFRSbiv. Neutralizing antibody titers against HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi, SEOV vaccine strain L99, and three representative epidemic strains from different genotypes (HTNV: SX26, SEOV: LN03 and FJ-17) were measured using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay-based microneutralization test (MN-ELISA). HV-neutralizing antibodies were detected from all the selected serum samples. Among HFRS patients, 47.92% (23/48) were identified as HTNV infection, 27.08% (13/48) were with SEOV infection, and 25% (12/48) were untypable. There is a significant difference in the titers of neutralizing antibodies against vaccine strains and epidemic strains detected in the serum samples. For HTNV, both patient and vaccinee sera exhibited significantly higher geometric mean titer (GMT) against vaccine strain 84FLi than against epidemic strain SX26 (1:386.08 vs. 1:223.04, P < 0.001; 1:137.94 vs. 1:110.37, P < 0.05, respectively). For SEOV, patient sera showed significantly lower GMT against vaccine strain L99 than against epidemic strain LN03 (1:177.02 vs. 1:297.71, P < 0.01), and vaccinee sera showed significantly lower GMT against L99 than against epidemic strain FJ-17 (1:97.52 vs. 1:243.71, P < 0.001). Significant immunogenicity heterogeneity was observed between SEOV epidemic strains LN03 and FJ-17. Conclusions/significance The genetic diversity and immunogenicity of HV, which causes HFRS, have certain geographical regional characteristics. The levels of cross neutralizing antibodies induced by infection of HV from different genotypes may vary significantly, but still provide sufficient cross protection. The HFRSbiv currently used in China could induce broad neutralizing antibody, the cross-protective efficacy might vary against different circulating strains and genotypes. It is of great significance to strengthen the monitoring of genetic characteristics of regional specific circulating viral strains, regularly evaluate the matching degree between vaccine protection effectiveness and epidemic strains, predict and evaluate the transmission and pathogenic risks of HV, and timely optimize HFRS prevention and control strategies and measures. Author summary Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by HV remains a serious threat to global public health security, with its epidemic scope continuing to expand. After more than 20 years of application in China, HFRS bivalent inactivated vaccine (HFRSbiv) has been proven to effectively prevent HFRS. However, the evolution and mutation of the virus pose challenges to this specific prevention and control measure. In this study, the levels of neutralizing antibodies against the vaccine strains and the current circulating virus strains in the panel of sera collected from confirmed HFRS patients at convalescent phase and adults who had received standardized immunization with HFRSbiv were evaluated. There are significant differences in the immunogenicity of cross protection induced by locally prevalent HV strains and vaccine strains (HTNV 84FLi and SEOV L99), which suggested that the effectiveness of HFRSbiv may vary in different parts of China. Our findings highlight the importance of the monitoring of genetic characteristics and immunogenicity of regional specific circulating viral strains to predict and evaluate the transmission and pathogenic risks for timely optimization of HFRS prevention and control strategies and measures. The viruses are distributed globally, and approximately 200,000 cases are reported annually, posing a persistent threat to human health [1]. In China, Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are the causative agents of HFRS, and the infection has a relatively wide distribution, with the highest annual reported cases exceeding 110000 in 1980s [2]. Although the annual incidence of HFRS had significantly decreased and maintained a low level in the last two decades, the geographical distribution range of Hantavirus (HV) infection had shown an expanding trend, and the virus presents a more abundant genetic diversity [3]. HV are predominantly hosted by rodents and exhibit strict host specificity, each hantavirus species is primarily carried and transmitted by one or several closely related reservoir hosts [4]. Virus–host adaptive evolution is influenced by ecological environments, host switching events, and gene selection pressures, contributing to the genetic diversity of hantaviruses. Moreover, as segmented RNA viruses, HV possess the capacity for genetic reassortment, enabling the exchange of genomic segments between two parental viruses co-infecting the same cell, thereby generating progeny viruses genetically distinct from both parents [5]. The frequency of segment exchange and the co-infection rate within the same host cell affect the success of genomic reassortment [6]. With the rapid development of laboratory testing technology and the expansion of pathogen monitoring scope, new HV strains continued to be discovered, presenting rich genetic diversity with regional characteristics in China [3,7]. papers.title: Genomic stasis during a person-to-person Andes virus outbreak, and nucleoprotein and glycoprotein conservation across the hantaviruses: analysis code and derived data
papers.abstract: Analysis code and derived data from a study of genomic stasis during a person-to-person Andes virus outbreak, and of nucleoprotein and glycoprotein conservation across the hantaviruses. The record contains, in nine data sections plus a code tree: 51 human tissue-specific codon adaptation index (CAI) weight tables built from Human Protein Atlas consensus expression; high-confidence tRNA gene sets and full-genome codon usage tables for five hantavirus reservoir hosts (Peromyscus maniculatus, Myodes glareolus, Talpa europaea, Sorex araneus, Sigmodon hispidus); protein-guided codon alignments of the nucleoprotein (S) and glycoprotein precursor (M) coding sequences of 22 hantavirus species (18 Orthohantavirus, two Thottimvirus, two Mobatvirus), with manifests, species label tables and alignment QC; the maximum-likelihood trees for both segments; the per-patient and per-segment open reading frame sets for the 28 patients of the 2018-2019 Epuyen Andes virus person-to-person outbreak; the pairwise divergence tables under three estimators, the exact species-label permutation tests, and the codeml control files and outputs for the branch models reported in this study; the within-species nucleotide-diversity table with its power and minimum-detectable-effect analysis; and the human codon usage and tRNA reference tables against which all CAI and codon co-adaptation values in this study are computed. The root README.md documents every section, gives the software versions used, and records three methodological cautions that are the parts of this work most likely to be reused: the tRNAscan-SE EukHighConfidenceFilter requirement, why a codon usage table must not be built from a few hundred GenBank CDS, and the per-amino-acid-family weight normalisation that a CAI implementation must apply. Scope note: this is a focused analysis package, not a project archive. Large third-party inputs (NCBI genome CDS sets, GenBank flatfile harvests, the Human Protein Atlas consensus matrix) are not redistributed; the manifests and download scripts included here retrieve them by accession. Derived per-sequence CAI scores are not deposited as tables, because they are recomputable from the deposited reference tables, sequences and code. Data are released under CC-BY-4.0. The code/ folder carries its own MIT licence (code/LICENCE_CODE.txt), matching the licence stated for the project repository.

papers.title: CD8+ regulatory T cells limit immunopathology but impair viral clearance in Hantaan virus infection.
papers.abstract: In hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV), virus-specific CD8+ T cells mediate both viral clearance and immunopathology. Here, we characterized a CD8+ regulatory T cell (Treg) subset restricted by HLA-E (and its murine ortholog Qa-1) in HFRS patients and in a murine HTNV infection model. CD8+ Tregs (CD122+Eomes+CD49dloKIR+), a subset substantially enriched for HLA-E-restricted T cells, were significantly reduced in peripheral blood of HFRS patients and displayed a terminally differentiated profile with elevated expression of KLRG-1, NKG2A, CTLA-4, and Fas-L, correlating with disease severity. Two HTNV glycoprotein-derived nonapeptides that bound Qa-1 were identified. Following immunization with the identified HTNV peptides and subsequent HTNV challenge, wild-type (WT) mice showed attenuated renal immunopathology, whereas D227K knock-in mice (with disrupted Qa-1-CD8/TCR interaction) showed enhanced viral clearance in the spleen and kidney but exacerbated renal immunopathology. Mechanistically, Qa-1-restricted CD8+ Tregs from WT mice suppressed effector CD8+ T cell proliferation in a peptide-specific, CD8/TCR-dependent manner via enhanced TGF-β secretion. Strikingly, D227K mutation dichotomously reshaped Treg phenotype: bulk polyclonal CD8+ Tregs displayed compensatory upregulation of inhibitory receptors (NKG2A, CTLA-4, PD-1) and TGF-β, whereas epitope-specific CD8+ Tregs showed impaired antigen-specific suppressive function and attenuated TGF-β production. Collectively, these findings indicate that HLA-E/Qa-1-restricted CD8+ Tregs can restrain immunopathology during HTNV infection, potentially at the cost of delayed viral elimination. Modulation of this axis may provide insights for therapeutic strategies in HFRS and related viral hemorrhagic fevers.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS caused by Hantaan virus involves CD8+ T cells that drive both clearance and pathology (A1). Methods: Researchers characterized HLA‑E‑restricted CD8+ Tregs in patients and a murine HTNV model, and immunized wild‑type and D227K mice with HTNV peptides before challenge (A2, A5). Limitations: Only abstract information is available; sample size and detailed methods are not reported (abstract_only).

Volume 32, Number 12—December 2026 Dispatch Rat Hepatitis E Virus and Seoul Hantavirus in Pet Rats, Germany Suggested citation for this article Abstract Pet rats represent a reservoir of multiple zoonotic pathogens. We demonstrated that pet rats, previously confirmed to be Seoul orthohantavirus–infected and involved in human infections in Germany, were concurrently infected with rat hepatitis E virus. The high degree of rat hepatitis E virus sequence identity suggests a single incursion event. Despite being closely associated with human settlements for much of recent human history, brown rats (Rattus norvegicus) were not domesticated as pets until the 17th and 18th Centuries in Japan (1). Wild brown rats, which are prolific synanthropic pests, harbor a great diversity of zoonotic agents (2,3). Pet rats, the domesticated form of brown rats, have likewise been associated with outbreaks of Leptospira spp. (4), Seoul virus (SEOV; Orthohantavirus seoulense) (5), and cowpox virus (6). SEOV is a zoonotic hantavirus found in both wild and pet rats globally (7). In Germany, pet rats have been linked to 4 detections of cases of human SEOV infection (5,8,9). Additional zoonotic pathogens in wild rats include the human pathogenic hepatitis E virus (HEV; Paslahepevirus balayani) and rat hepatitis E virus (rHEV; Rocahepevirus ratti). HEV is one of the main causative agents of acute hepatitis in humans worldwide and is typically transmitted through the fecal–oral route, consumption of undercooked pork, or blood and organ transplants. rHEV has been detected in wild brown rats and black rats (Rattus rattus) worldwide and is now recognized as a novel human pathogen causing acute and chronic hepatitis (10,11). Rats (Rattus spp.) are reservoirs of rHEV but have also been reported to be incidentally infected with genotype HEV-3 (12). To assess the presence of rHEV, HEV-3, and other related hepeviruses, as well as potential co-infection with SEOV and tissue distribution of hepevirus RNA and SEOV antigen in SEOV-infected and noninfected pet rats, we screened samples from 13 pet rats associated with 3 SEOV detections in human patients in Germany by molecular and serologic assays. Of those 13 pet rats, 11 tested positive for SEOV RNA in previous studies (5,9) (Appendix Table 1). We extracted RNA from liver tissue and screened it by a nested broad-spectrum reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) capable of detecting multiple HEV genotypes and rHEV (Appendix). By sequencing the RT-PCR products, we identified rHEV RNA in 3 of the 13 pet rats (KS19/1354, KS19/2196, and KS22/001), a finding further confirmed by rHEV-specific real-time RT-PCR (Appendix Table 1). The 3 pet rats, which were previously shown to be infected by SEOV (Appendix Table 1), came from 3 different owners; 2 rats were obtained from the same vendor and the source for the third rat was unknown (5,8,9). The 276 nt-long open reading frame (ORF) 1 and corresponding amino acid (aa) sequences of rHEV from the 3 pet rats were nearly identical (99.15%–100%) (Appendix Table 2). For further sequence comparisons and phylogenetic analyses, we downloaded 91 partial and 60 complete genome rHEV sequences from GenBank (Figure). In addition, we determined short ORF1 sequences of 12 wild brown rats from Rotterdam (n = 8) and Amsterdam (n = 4) (the Netherlands) that previously tested positive for rHEV RNA (2). Phylogenetic analysis demonstrated that the 3 pet rat–derived sequences were highly similar (98.55%–98.91%) to a wild rat–derived rHEV sequence from Rotterdam (M226) (Figure, panel A). A multiplex serology approach using bead-based Luminex technology (R&D Systems, https://www.rndsystems.com) (Appendix) detected rHEV-reactive antibodies in 12 of 13 pet rat blood samples; 3 of those 12 samples also showed reactivity to HEV-3 antigen (Appendix Table 1). Subsequent Western blot analysis using the same 2 antigens mainly supported multiplex serology results: 11 of 12 multiplex serology–positive samples also tested positive for rHEV. Of the 11 seropositive samples, 10 also reacted in the Western blot assay with the HEV-3 antigen (Appendix Table 1, Figure 1). That high seroprevalence suggests widespread circulation in pet rat breeding facilities, which should be confirmed using a larger sample size. In all 3 rHEV RNA–positive pet rats, rHEV-reactive antibodies were detected by multiplex serology. Differences in the results of multiplex serology and Western blot assay can be explained by differences in the epitope presentation and sensitivity of both assays. We obtained near-full rHEV genome sequences from the 3 pet rats from Germany (KS19/1354, KS19/2196, and KS22/001) and from 3 of the wild brown rats from the Netherlands by using a combination of high-throughput sequencing and RT-PCR–based sequence determination of the hypervariable genome region. The wild brown rats (M226, M268, and M186) from Rotterdam were selected for different levels of ORF1 sequence similarity to the 3 pet rat–derived sequences (Figure, panel A). The rHEV full genome sequences from the 3 pet rats were >99.7% identical, and nucleotide and amino acid sequences of all 4 ORFs and encoded proteins were >99.2% identical (Appendix Table 2). As in ORF1, the full genomes from the 3 German pet rats were most similar to the sequence from wild brown rat M226 from Rotterdam (full sequence >99.2% identical; each ORF >98.3%) (Appendix Table 3) and clustered with that sequence in the phylogeny (Figure, panel B). The most closely related rHEV sequences from Germany were detected in wild brown rats from Hamburg (Figure, panel B). The only sequence from a human patient in Germany (13) clustered among sequences from wild brown rats from Berlin, separate from the pet rat sequences (Figure, panel B; Appendix Table 3). On the basis of the complete coding sequences of pet rat–derived rHEV, we selected probe sequences to detect rHEV RNA through in situ hybridization in formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissues of the pet rats mounted on adhesive microscope slides (Appendix). We clearly detected a disseminated in situ hybridization signal using brightfield microscopy in the livers (hepatocytes) of rats KS19/1354, KS19/2196, and KS22/001, confirming the rHEV quantitative RT-PCR results (Appendix Table 1, Figure 2). In addition, we detected an oligofocal in situ hybridization signal in the spleen of pet rat KS22/001 and in the intestinal lumen of pet rat KS19/1354. We detected no signal in the other tissues tested (Appendix Table 4). Nucleocapsid protein immunohistochemistry analysis of the rHEV-SEOV coinfected pet rats KS19/1354, KS19/2196, and KS22/001 demonstrated SEOV antigen in multiple organs, predominantly the kidney and brain; antigen was detected less frequently in the spleen, intestine, liver, and lung (Appendix Tables 1, 3, Figure 2). That distribution is consistent with the previously described widespread endothelial tropism of SEOV in naturally infected wild rats and experimentally infected laboratory rats (14). In our study, advanced autolysis limited the assessment of pathological changes. We could not assess colocalization of both viruses because of insufficient tissue material. The co-infection of pet rats with the zoonotic pathogens SEOV and ratHEV and the rat-to-human transmission of SEOV in those cases (8,9) highlights a public health concern posed by pet rats. Unfortunately, the owners of the pet rats did not consent to providing blood samples; therefore, their rHEV serologic status could not be assessed. The near-identical rHEV sequences in the pet rats indicate a single incursion event consistent with potentially being independently obtained from the same vendor in Germany (5). The close similarity between the pet rat rHEV sequences and a wild rat–derived sequence from the Netherlands might indicate a wild rat origin of pet rat rHEV, further circulation by pet rat trade, and (at least mostly) uncoupled dynamics of rHEV in wild and captive rats. Owners and general practitioners should be aware of potential zoonotic risks associated with pet rats so that preventive hygienic measures can be taken and correct diagnosis supported. Dr. Mehl is a postdoctoral researcher at the Friedrich-Loeffler-Institut in Greifswald-Insel Riems, Germany. His research interests include the interplay between pathogen and host ecology, with a focus on small mammals. Acknowledgments We thank Dörte Kaufmann, Stephan Drewes, Elisabeth Striese, Stephanie Hübl, Silvia Schuparis, Christiane Klier, and Simon Dökel for their support. Ethical approval was not required for this investigation because it was conducted under the German Protection against Infection Act with the aim of investigating transmission routes and halting further spread of infection. All novel sequences were uploaded to GenBank (accession nos. PZ581217–22 and PZ583560–71). Funding was provided through the German Center for Infection Research, Thematical Translation Unit “Emerging Infections” (grant no. 01.808_00). C.M. acknowledges intramural funding by Friedrich-Loeffler-Institut, and R.J. acknowledges intramural funding by German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment. analysis.background: Pet rats are reservoirs of multiple zoonotic pathogens, including Seoul orthohantavirus (SEOV) and rat hepatitis E virus (rHEV). SEOV has caused human infections in Germany, and rHEV is a novel human pathogen causing acute and chronic hepatitis.
analysis.methods: Thirteen pet rats linked to three human SEOV cases were sampled; liver RNA was screened by nested broad‑spectrum RT‑PCR and confirmed by rHEV‑specific real‑time RT‑PCR. Serology used multiplex Luminex bead assay and Western blot with rHEV and HEV‑3 antigens. Near‑full rHEV genomes were obtained by high‑throughput sequencing and RT‑PCR, and phylogenetic analysis compared them to GenBank sequences.
analysis.results: rHEV RNA was detected in 3 of 13 rats; their ORF1 sequences were 99.15–100% identical and closely related (98.55–98.91%) to a Rotterdam wild‑rat rHEV. Serology showed rHEV antibodies in 12/13 rats, with 3 also reactive to HEV‑3; all RNA‑positive rats were seropositive.
analysis.contribution: The study reveals concurrent SEOV and rHEV infection in pet rats, indicating a single incursion event and widespread circulation in breeding facilities, underscoring a potential zoonotic risk to humans.
analysis.limitations: The small sample size limits generalizability; larger studies are needed to confirm prevalence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Pet rats are reservoirs of zoonotic pathogens such as SEOV and rHEV, the latter being a novel human hepatitis agent. Methods: Thirteen SEOV‑positive pet rats from Germany were screened for rHEV and HEV‑3 by nested RT‑PCR, real‑time RT‑PCR, Luminex serology, and Western blot; near‑full rHEV genomes were sequenced and phylogenetically compared. Results: rHEV RNA was found in 3 rats, whose sequences were nearly identical and closely related to a Rotterdam wild‑rat rHEV; 12/13 rats had rHEV antibodies, 3 also reacted to HEV‑3, and all RNA‑positive rats were seropositive. Contribution: The findings show concurrent SEOV and rHEV infection in pet rats, suggesting a single incursion and widespread circulation in breeding facilities, highlighting zoonotic risk. Limitations: Small sample size limits generalizability; larger studies are needed to confirm prevalence.

papers.title_zh: 德国宠物鼠中的鼠乙型肝炎病毒和首尔病毒 汉坦病毒

analysis_zh.background: 宠物鼠是多种人畜共患病原体的储存宿主,包括首尔病毒 正汉坦病毒 (SEOV) 和鼠肝炎E病毒 (rHEV)。SEOV 曾在德国引起人类感染,而 rHEV 是一种引起急性和慢性肝炎的新型人类病原体。
analysis_zh.methods: 对与三例人类 SEOV 病例相关的13只宠物鼠进行了采样;通过嵌套广谱 RT-PCR 对肝脏 RNA 进行筛查,并通过 rHEV 特异性实时 RT-PCR 进行确认。血清学检测采用多重 Luminex 磁珠法以及使用 rHEV 和 HEV-3 抗原的 Western blot。通过高通量测序和 RT-PCR 获得了近全长 rHEV 基因组,并通过系统发育分析将其与 GenBank 序列进行比较。
analysis_zh.results: 在13只鼠中的3只中检测到 rHEV RNA;其 ORF1 序列具有 99.15–100% 的同源性,并与鹿特丹野生鼠 rHEV 密切相关(98.55–98.91%)。血清学检测显示 12/13 只鼠存在 rHEV 抗体,其中3只对 HEV-3 也有反应;所有 RNA 阳性的鼠均为血清学阳性。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该研究揭示了宠物鼠中 SEOV 和 rHEV 的并发感染,表明存在单一的入侵事件以及在繁育设施中的广泛传播,凸显了对人类的潜在人畜共患风险。
analysis_zh.limitations: 样本量小限制了普遍性;需要更大规模的研究来确认流行率。

papers.title: An NCG mouse model of Hantaan virus reveals systemic infection and organ-specific cellular tropism
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV) is primarily endemic across Eurasia, posing a severe threat of renal failure and mortality. The mechanisms of HTNV infection remain poorly understood, largely due to the lack of susceptible animal models. In this study, we established a systemic HTNV infection mouse model using highly immunodeficient NCG mice. Following viral inoculation, we assessed viral loads via quantitative RT-PCR and mapped cellular tropism and co-localization of HTNV with potential receptors using immunofluorescence staining. While histopathological lesions were subclinical, HTNV-infected NCG mice exhibited robust viremia and sustained viral replication across multiple organs, including the kidney, lung, spleen, reproductive organs, and liver. HTNV exhibited distinct organ-specific cellular tropism in vivo, predominantly targeting fibroblasts and interstitial cells of the renal collecting duct in the kidney, alveolar epithelial cells and macrophages in the lung, and broadly infecting multiple cell populations in the brain and ovary. Co-localization analyses indicated HTNV infection might be associated with distinct entry receptors across target organs: potentially ITGB1 and gC1qR in specific renal cells, and ITGB1 and ITGB2 in pulmonary AT1 cells and macrophages, respectively. These findings demonstrate that NCG mouse is a valuable in vivo model for studying HTNV replication and systemic dissemination.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaan virus causes severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome across Eurasia, but infection mechanisms are unclear due to lack of models. Contribution: The NCG mouse is presented as a useful model for studying HTNV replication and dissemination. Limitations: Only an abstract is available; detailed limitations are not reported.

papers.title_zh: NCG 小鼠模型 汉滩病毒 揭示系统性感染和器官特异性细胞嗜性

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热 由 汉滩病毒 引起,已在欧亚大陆普遍流行,可导致肾衰竭和死亡;汉滩病毒感染机制尚不清楚,原因是缺乏易感动物模型。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者在高度免疫缺陷的 NCG 小鼠中建立了系统性汉滩病毒感染模型,使用定量 RT-PCR 测定病毒载量,并通过免疫荧光染色绘制细胞受体共定位与细胞亲和性。
analysis_zh.results: HTNV感染的NCG小鼠表现出强烈的血病毒血症,并在肾、肺、脾、生殖器官和肝脏中持续复制;病毒显示器官特异性嗜性,主要感染肾集合管成纤维细胞、肺泡上皮细胞和巨噬细胞,以及多种脑和卵巢细胞类型;共定位提示ITGB1、gC1qR和ITGB2可能作为潜在的入侵受体。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究表明,NCG小鼠是研究HTNV复制、系统性传播及器官特异性细胞靶点的有价值的体内模型。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供了摘要;未在所提供的证据中报告详细的方法学和实验局限性。

papers.title: Molecular evolution of Andes virus lineages leading to recent human outbreaks
papers.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV) is exceptional among hantaviruses in its capacity for person-to-person transmission, but whether outbreaks reflect recent viral adaptation or emergence of pre-existing reservoir lineages remains unclear. We generated paired blood- and nasal-derived genomes from the MV Hondius outbreak and integrated them with a segment-linked collection of human- and rodent-derived ANDV sequences, including incomplete genomes. We developed a linkage-informed missing-segment framework that preserves isolate identity, sampling time, and cross-segment placement without imputing nucleotide states, enabling sensitivity analyses of patchy segment coverage. Across five human outbreaks, dated phylogenies placed outbreak lineages independently within geographically structured reservoir diversity, with closest sampled ancestry predating detection. Time-dependent-rate analyses indicated a deeper reservoir-associated history, while mutation reconstruction, selection tests, branch-rate comparisons, and structural mapping found no recurrent adaptive transition preceding human transmission. MV Hondius samples showed minimal consensus-level diversification. These results shift attention from repeated recent adaptation toward deeper lineage properties and ecological opportunity.

We developed a linkage-informed missing-segment framework that preserves isolate identity, sampling time, and cross-segment placement without imputing nucleotide states, enabling sensitivity analyses of patchy segment coverage. Across five human outbreaks, dated phylogenies placed outbreak lineages independently within geographically structured reservoir diversity, with closest sampled ancestry predating detection. Time-dependent-rate analyses indicated a deeper reservoir-associated history, while mutation reconstruction, selection tests, branch-rate comparisons, and structural mapping found no recurrent adaptive transition preceding human transmission. MV Hondius samples showed minimal consensus-level diversification. These results shift attention from repeated recent adaptation toward deeper lineage properties and ecological opportunity.

(spyros.lytras@pasteur.fr); M.G. (mahan.ghafari@biology.ox.ac.uk) 16 Abstract 17 Andes virus (ANDV) is exceptional among hantaviruses in its capacity for person-to- 18 person transmission, but whether outbreaks reflect recent viral adaptation or emergence 19 of pre-existing reservoir lineages remains unclear. We generated paired blood- and nasal- 20 derived genomes from the MV Hondius outbreak and integrated them with a segment- 21 linked collection of human- and rodent-derived ANDV sequences, including incomplete 22 genomes. We developed a linkage-informed missing-segment framework that preserves 23 isolate identity, sampling time, and cross-segment placement without imputing nucleotide 24 states, enabling sensitivity analyses of patchy segment coverage. Across five human 25 outbreaks, dated phylogenies placed outbreak lineages independently within 26 geographically structured reservoir diversity, with closest sampled ancestry predating 27 detection. Time-dependent-rate analyses indicated a deeper reservoir-associated history, 28 while mutation reconstruction, selection tests, branch-rate comparisons, and structural 29 mapping found no recurrent adaptive transition preceding human transmission. MV 30 Hondius samples showed minimal consensus-level diversification. These results shift 31 attention from repeated recent adaptation toward deeper lineage properties and 32 ecological opportunity. 33 Introduction 34 Andes hantavirus (ANDV) causes severe hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome and is 35 unusual among hantaviruses in its capacity for documented person-to-person 36 transmission1. ANDV has a tripartite negative-sense single-stranded RNA genome in 37 which the S segment encodes the nucleoprotein, the M segment encodes the 38 glycoprotein precursor that gives rise to Gn and Gc, and the L segment encodes the RNA- 39 dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp)2. Historical sequencing is uneven across these 40 segments, with many isolates represented by only one or two segments and some M- 41 segment records available only as partial Gn/Gc sequences with separate accessions. 42 ANDV circulates primarily in the long-tailed colilargo (Oligoryzomys longicaudatus), with 43 occasional detection in other rodents (e.g. Loxodontomys micropus, Abrothrix longipilis), 44 and repeatedly spill over into humans in Argentina and Chile3,4. The 2018-2019 Epuyén 45 outbreak5 and the 2026 MV Hondius-associated outbreak have therefore raised a central 46 question: are ANDV outbreaks involving person-to-person transmission driven by the 47 recent adaptive viral changes, or by the ecological emergence of pre-existing reservoir 48 lineages already capable of limited human transmission? Previous comparative work 49 proposed candidate mutations associated with person-to-person transmission6, but 50 whether independent outbreaks share a recurrent recent adaptive transition has not been 51 tested systematically. 52 These alternatives make different evolutionary predictions. Under a model of recent 53 adaptive emergence, independently arising human outbreaks should repeatedly be 54 preceded by one or more signatures of viral adaptation. These may include features such 55 as accelerated nonsynonymous evolution, signals of positive selection on outbreak- 56 lineage ancestral branches, convergent amino acid changes, or recurrent perturbation of 57 viral structures involved in entry, replication, immune evasion, or antigenicity. Under an 58 ecological-emergence model, outbreak lineages should instead be distributed across 59 standing reservoir diversity, retain strong geographic structure, and lack a reproducible 60 genomic transition immediately before their detection in humans. 61 For many emerging zoonoses, genomic epidemiology focuses on reconstructing 62 transmission chains after detection in humans. For reservoir-borne viruses, however, the 63 deeper question is often whether the human outbreak lineage can be placed within known 64 animal diversity and whether the branch leading to human emergence shows evidence 65 of accelerated or adaptive evolution. 66 This is particularly challenging for ANDV, for which available genomic data are sparse 67 and unevenly sampled across human and rodent hosts7. Available sequences include 68 known human outbreak clusters, rodent-associated genomes, and ANDV-like sequences 69 that have not always been consistently classified within major clades. Historical isolates 70 are also frequently represented by incomplete segment sets, resulting in substantial 71 differences in sequence availability across segments and sampling dates. These 72 characteristics can complicate molecular dating, as uneven temporal and host sampling 73 can distort the available temporal signal, while incomplete segment sampling and 74 uncertainty in clade classification can influence the inferred phylogenetic structure. 75 Together, these factors may affect evolutionary-rate and divergence-time estimates, and 76 potentially bias inferences about outbreak origins. 77 Here, we use the MV Hondius 2026 outbreak as an entry point into a broader comparative 78 analysis of ANDV evolution. We generated a paired blood- and nasal-derived S, M, and 79 L segment sequence from the outbreak and integrated them with a segment-linked 80 collection of public human, rodent, and ANDV-like sequences, including incomplete and 81 partial genomes. We first reconstruct population-level diversity and introduce a linkage- 82 informed missing-segment framework for retaining sampled viruses in segment 83 alignments when a linked segment is unavailable. We then systematically infer molecular 84 rate estimates, evaluate the presence of time-dependent rate variation across nested 85 datasets and apply the Prisoner of War (PoW) model8 to examine deeper evolutionary 86 timelines of ANDV. Against this macroevolutionary background, we compare the 87 evolutionary emergence of MV Hondius outbreak with four earlier outbreaks involving 88 documented human-to-human transmission: i) a household and nosocomial transmission 89 chain in Southern Chile with five human infections in 2011 (Chile 2011)9 , ii) a three- 90 person transmission cluster in Argentina in 2014 (Argentina 2014)10 , iii) the largest known 91 ANDV outbreak with 34 confirmed infections in Argentina in 2018-2019 (Epuyén 92 2018/19)5, and iv) a two-person family cluster from Chile in 2024 (Chile 2024)11. We then 93 identify the closest sampled relatives and geographic context of each outbreak lineage, 94 reconstruct their evolutionary ancestry, and identify coding substitutions that arose along 95 the ancestral branch leading to each outbreak. By combining these reconstructions with 96 branch-rate, codon-selection, and structural analyses, we directly test whether repeated 97 human outbreaks share evidence of recent adaptive emergence while explicitly 98 accounting for the patchiness of the available genomic records. 99 Results 100 Phylogenetic placement and molecular dating of recorded ANDV human outbreaks 101 To best characterise the broader diversity that ANDV sits in, we first reconstructed 102 maximum-likelihood phylogenies for all publicly available S, M and L genome segments 103 of the Orthohantavirus andesense (Supplementary Figures 1-3). Consistent with 104 previous studies6, the five recorded human-to-human outbreak lineages fell within the 105 four main ANDV clades and were embedded within the broader rodent-associated ANDV 106 diversity. Our expanded curation additionally retains incomplete and partial genome 107 records, including rodent-derived isolates and the Chile 2011 human outbreak 4,9 that 108 would be lost by restricting analysis to complete three-segment genomes, thereby 109 broadening the reservoir context available for each outbreak. The closest sampled 110 relatives of the outbreak lineages were regionally structured. MV Hondius 2026 and Chile 111 2024 clustered within ANDV clade 3, together with rodent-derived (O. longicaudatus) 112 sequences4 and isolated human-infection sequences from Valdivia, Los Ríos, and San 113 Martín de los Andes, Neuquén, together with related Neuquén sequences9. This pattern 114 is consistent with a cross-border southern Chile-northern Patagonia assemblage rather 115 than a source confined to one national surveillance system (Figure 1A, Supplementary 116 Figures 1-3). The Argentina 2014 and Epuyén 2018/19 lineages were placed within 117 ANDV clade 2, whereas Chile 2011 fell within clade 1. No human-to-human transmission 118 has been documented yet for members of ANDV clade 4 (which contains the reference 119 ANDV genome, strain Chile-97178692), although it contains genomes derived from 120 isolated human infections. Several rodent-derived sequences fell within ANDV diversity 121 but outside clades 1-4. In particular, two well-supported groups were recovered in M and 122 S segments. Several other isolates also occupied positions outside clades 1-4, but these 123 placements were more weakly supported and/or inconsistent among genome segments. 124 These sequences may represent additional, previously under-recognised lineages of 125 ANDV. We refer to all of these sequences and clusters as “unclassified” (Supplementary 126 Figures 1-3). 127 The nearest sampled relatives of each outbreak lineage differed among genome 128 segments, owing to uneven sequence availability across the segmented genome (Figure 129 1). We refer to these non-outbreak human- or rodent-derived nearest relatives as 130 comparator sequences, because they provide the phylogenetic context for placing 131 outbreak lineages within broader ANDV diversity. The M segment contained the richest 132 set of nearby comparators for all outbreak lineages (total of 78 available ANDV M 133 segment sequences), followed by the S segment (70 available ANDV sequences). The L 134 segment had fewer nearby comparators and lacked equivalent closely related rodent- 135 derived sequences, limiting reservoir-inclusive inference (50 available ANDV sequences). 136 These differences in segment availability are central to the molecular dating problem 137 addressed below: although sequences from different segments may be linked to the same 138 isolate, observed-sequence-only alignments cannot represent that linkage when one or 139 more segments are missing. 140 Analysing only taxa with observed sequence data in each segment therefore produced 141 segment-specific datasets with different taxonomic compositions and, for a small subset 142 of clades, poorly resolved or unstable time trees. Rather than discarding incompletely 143 sequenced isolates, we developed a linkage-informed missing-segment representation 144 to retain known linkage without imputing sequence states (see Methods). If a sampled 145 virus had an observed sequence for at least one segment but lacked another, the missing 146 segment was represented by a genetically non-informative sequence (i.e., an all-N 147 sequence of the appropriate length) and assigned the same isolate identity and sampling 148 date. Its placement was constrained to the clade or internal relationship supported by the 149 linked observed segment(s), while unconstrained relationships remained estimated from 150 the segment-specific data. The approach therefore carries known linkage, sampling time, 151 and explicit cross-segment topology assumptions; it does not reconstruct the missing 152 sequence, and its assumptions can be violated by reassortment or uncertainty in the 153 constrained topology. We accordingly interpret linkage-informed estimates alongside the 154 observed-sequence dataset. 155 Observed-sequence S, M, and L trees placed outbreak-associated lineages and their 156 nearest comparators in broadly congruent positions (Figure 1A). Because missing- 157 segment taxa are constrained by linked segments, we assessed reassortment only in 158 observed-sequence trees. We found no well-supported segment discordance involving 159 the five outbreak lineages or their closest comparators, with the caveat that only M- 160 segment data are available for Chile 2011. Few placements differed among segments, 161 but most involved weakly supported nodes (posterior probability <0.8). Thus, 162 reassortment may have partly contributed to ANDV evolution, but it does not affect the 163 placement of the recent outbreak lineages analysed here. 164 Molecular clock behaviour and deeper evolutionary history of ANDV 165 We next systematically evaluated temporal signal and time-dependent rate variation 166 across nested ANDV datasets. For each genome segment, we analysed progressively 167 broader phylogenetic subsets comprising clade 2 alone; a combined clade 1 + clade 3 168 dataset containing only clades 1 and 3; clades 1-3 containing clades 1, 2 and 3; and 169 clades 1-4 containing all four major ANDV clades. Bayesian Evaluation of Temporal 170 Signal (BETS)12 compared heterochronous models incorporating the observed sampling 171 dates with otherwise equivalent isochronous models in which all tips were assigned the 172 same date (Methods). BETS supported the presence of temporal signal for all M- 173 segment datasets, and most S-segment datasets (except the clade1 + clade 3 datasets). 174 Temporal signal was weaker for the L-segment, consistent with fewer sequences, lacking 175 signal for clade 2, clade 1 + clade 3, and clade 1-3 datasets (Supplementary Table 4). 176 However, the inclusion of linkage-informed missing-segment taxa and the associated 177 constraints on the tree topology stabilised the time-scaled phylogeny, produced a 178 consistent rate estimate across independent runs, and restored support for temporal 179 signal by BETS (see Supplementary Table 4). Because the missing-segment taxa add 180 no nucleotide states, this gain should be interpreted as improved use of known sampling 181 and linkage information rather than additional sequence evidence. This improvement was 182 particularly important for the more sparsely sampled L segment, where incomplete taxon 183 representation otherwise limited time-tree inference. 184 185 Figure 1. Time-scaled ancestry of the five documented ANDV human outbreaks across 186 genome segments. (A) Dated maximum clade credibility trees for the L, S, and M coding 187 sequences. Genomes with sequences available for multiple segments are connected between 188 the phylogenies and coloured based on the ANDV clade they are part of. Sequences of the MV 189 Hondius 2026 outbreak reported in this study are highlighted in pink and followed by an asterisk. 190 Nodes with posterior support below 0.8 are annotated with pink dots and their posterior support 191 value is shown next to them. (B) Posterior distributions for the closest sampled common ancestor 192 of each outbreak lineage under three sampling configurations: observed-sequence-only datasets 193 (“Observed”), observed-sequence datasets retaining two representatives per outbreak (“2pO”), 194 and linkage-informed datasets containing missing-segment taxa (“Linkage-informed”; labelled 195 “All” in the panel). Horizontal lines show posterior medians and box limits show 95% highest 196 posterior density intervals. 197 198 Across the nested datasets, posterior evolutionary rate estimates declined as older and 199 more divergent ANDV diversity was incorporated (Figure 2A, Supplementary Table 5). 200 Clade 2 tended to produce the highest rate estimates, whereas broader clade 201 combinations produced lower estimates. This systematic decline in inferred rate with 202 increasing phylogenetic depth is consistent with time-dependent rate variation. Across 203 different sampling configurations, rate estimates were comparatively stable except where 204 topology uncertainty was substantial, as in L clades 1+3. By contrast, closest-sampled- 205 ancestor dates were more sensitive to comparator representation (Figure 1B). The 206 principal value of the linkage-informed analysis is therefore not added sequence evidence 207 or guaranteed precision, but explicit representation and testing of known cross-segment 208 linkage and topology assumptions under patchy segment coverage. 209 Time-dependent rate variation is well described in RNA viruses, with short-term 210 evolutionary-rate estimates often exceeding those inferred over deeper timescales13. In 211 RNA viruses, this can arise because recent datasets retain transient polymorphisms and 212 mildly deleterious mutations that are later removed by purifying selection8. This 213 interpretation is also consistent with our codon-based analyses, which indicate that 214 purifying selection dominates most coding regions of the ANDV genome. In ANDV, the 215 effect may be particularly apparent because older pre-outbreak human- and rodent- 216 derived sequences can remain genetically very similar to much more recent outbreak 217 lineages. Incorporating these older comparator sequences therefore increases the 218 temporal depth of the datase…

papers.title_zh: 近期人类暴发相关的安第斯病毒谱系的分子进化

analysis_zh.background: 安第斯病毒(ANDV)在汉坦病毒中因具有人际传播能力而独特,但尚不清楚疫情是源于近期病毒适应还是已有储存宿主系的出现。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究从2026年MV Hondius疫情中获取血液和鼻腔来源的配对基因组,并将其与人类和啮齿动物来源的安第斯病毒序列的节段关联集合相整合,采用基于关联的信息框架处理不完整的节段数据。
analysis_zh.results: 时间标定的系统发育树将五条人类疫情系定位于地理结构化的储存宿主多样性中,其祖先早于检测;分析未发现在人际传播前出现的重复适应性转变,且MV Hondius样本显示出极少的共识水平多样化。
analysis_zh.contribution: 这些发现将关注点从反复的近期适应转向更深层的系谱特性和生态机会,视其为导致安第斯病毒人际传播疫情的驱动因素。
analysis_zh.limitations: 该分析依赖于在人类和啮齿动物宿主间稀疏且采样不均的基因组数据,许多分离株仅有不完整的节段集合,这可能影响进化速率和分歧时间的估计。

papers.title: Hantaviruses at the human-animal-environment interface: a One Health review of rodent reservoirs, surveillance, and preparedness.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses maintained in small mammals cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. Exposure usually arises from contact with infected rodent excreta, so prevention depends on understanding reservoir ecology, human activities, and the settings in which they intersect. This structured narrative review synthesizes evidence on host relationships, exposure, clinical and laboratory recognition, genomic investigation, and One Health surveillance across several regions. We propose three risk-proportionate tiers: baseline readiness where evidence is sparse, enhanced investigation after a credible signal, and sustained integrated surveillance where transmission is established. Five shared functions are scaled across tiers: reservoir sampling, clinical recognition and referral testing, molecular characterization, occupational and environmental assessment, and cross-sector data review. Published outbreaks in Croatia and long-running surveillance in Panama illustrate how the decision logic could be applied, while the 2026 Andes virus cruise-ship event highlights the need for diagnostics and contact management. The framework provides a practical way to plan surveillance with limited resources, but its triggers, workload, and impact remain to be evaluated prospectively.

papers.title: Case Report: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by Seoul orthohantavirus mimicking severe acute pancreatitis: dynamic imaging evolution and pathogen confirmation by mNGS.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses, characterized by fever, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and capillary leak syndrome. Its atypical presentations can closely mimic acute pancreatitis (AP), posing substantial diagnostic challenges. CASE PRESENTATION: A 33-year-old man presented with fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. Initial computed tomography (CT) revealed peripancreatic and perirenal exudation suggestive of severe acute pancreatitis. He already had profound thrombocytopenia on admission (nadir 29 × 109/L), progressive renal impairment, hematuria, and proteinuria, without typical pancreatitis risk factors or elevated pancreatic enzymes. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated progressive retroperitoneal exudation with relatively mild pancreatic parenchymal changes and newly developed bilateral pleural effusion. Whole-blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus, with concurrent hepatitis B virus. The patient recovered fully with supportive care, intravenous immunoglobulin, and symptomatic treatment; pre-discharge ultrasound showed normal pancreatic morphology. CONCLUSION: Seoul orthohantavirus infection can closely mimic severe acute pancreatitis clinically and radiologically. Disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, and progressive retroperitoneal exudation with preserved pancreatic parenchyma are key diagnostic clues, and mNGS enables early definitive pathogen confirmation, facilitating appropriate management.

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses and can present atypically, closely mimicking acute pancreatitis (AP).
analysis.methods: A single 33‑year‑old male case was evaluated with clinical assessment, initial and contrast‑enhanced CT imaging, laboratory tests, and whole‑blood metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (mNGS) for pathogen detection.
analysis.results: The patient had fever, vomiting, diarrhea, profound thrombocytopenia (nadir 29 × 10⁹/L), renal impairment, hematuria, proteinuria, and no elevated pancreatic enzymes; CT suggested severe AP but showed mild pancreatic changes and progressive retroperitoneal exudation; mNGS identified high‑copy Seoul orthohantavirus (and hepatitis B virus); supportive care with IVIG led to full recovery and normal pancreatic morphology on pre‑discharge ultrasound.
analysis.contribution: The report demonstrates that Seoul orthohantavirus infection can closely resemble severe AP, highlights diagnostic clues (disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, preserved pancreas), and shows mNGS enables early definitive pathogen confirmation, guiding appropriate management.
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract of a single case is available; broader epidemiologic or therapeutic data are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS caused by orthohantaviruses can mimic acute pancreatitis. Methods: A 33‑year‑old man was assessed with CT imaging, labs, and whole‑blood mNGS. Results: He presented with fever, vomiting, diarrhea, severe thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and CT suggesting pancreatitis, but mNGS identified Seoul orthohantavirus; he recovered with supportive care and normal pancreas on follow‑up. Contribution: Highlights Seoul virus can imitate severe pancreatitis, identifies key diagnostic clues, and shows mNGS as a rapid diagnostic tool. Limitations: Only an abstract of a single case is provided; no broader data are reported.

papers.title_zh: 病例报告:由首尔 正汉坦病毒 引起的 肾综合征出血热 伪装为重症急性胰腺炎:动态影像演变及mNGS病原体确认。

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热(HFRS)是一种由 正汉坦病毒 引起的动物源性疾病,可表现为非典型,极易模拟急性胰腺炎(AP)。
analysis_zh.methods: 对一名33岁男性病例进行临床评估、常规及增强CT检查、实验室检测以及全血宏基因组下一代测序(mNGS)以检测病原体。
analysis_zh.results: 患者出现发热、呕吐、腹泻、严重血小板减少(最低值 29 × 109/L)、肾功能受损、血尿、蛋白尿,且胰酶未升高;CT提示严重急性胰腺炎但仅显示轻度胰腺改变和进行性后腹膜渗出;mNGS鉴定出高拷贝首尔病毒 正汉坦病毒(以及hepatitis B virus);给予IVIG等支持治疗后,患者完全恢复,出院前超声显示胰腺形态正常。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本报告显示首尔病毒 正汉坦病毒 感染可高度模拟严重急性胰腺炎,强调诊断线索(血小板显著下降、肾脏受累、胰腺保留),并证明mNGS能够早期明确病原体,指导恰当的治疗。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅有单例摘要可供参考,未提供更广泛的流行病学或治疗数据。

papers.title: Early warning indicators for severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) remains a significant public health concern, and early identification of severe cases is critical for improving outcomes. This review synthesizes recent advances in early warning indicators for severe HFRS. Clinically accessible indicators form the basis of early risk stratification. Key bedside signs such as high fever, severe gastrointestinal symptoms, altered mental status, and overt bleeding tendency, together with routine laboratory parameters including thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis, and elevated procalcitonin, have consistently shown robust predictive value for disease severity and mortality. Immunological markers provide mechanistic insight that also supports early identification of severe HFRS, as reflected by a core cytokine imbalance, impaired antigen-specific T- and B-cell responses, and aberrant activation of monocytes, neutrophils, and the complement system. Emerging biomarkers of endothelial barrier disruption, early renal tubular injury, oxidative stress, and metabolic dysregulation may further enhance predictive capacity. Despite these advances, challenges remain regarding external validation and clinical translation. Future research should focus on establishing standardized, multicenter-validated early warning systems to enable precise management of severe HFRS.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS is a major public health issue and early detection of severe cases is vital. Main directions: The review covers clinical signs, routine labs, immunological and emerging biomarkers as early warning tools. Current state: Bedside signs and labs reliably predict severity, and immune dysregulation offers mechanistic insight. Gaps: Validation and clinical translation remain limited. Future research: Standardized, multicenter‑validated early warning systems are needed.

papers.title_zh: 严重肾综合征出血热的早期预警指标。

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热(HFRS)仍然是重大公共卫生问题,及早识别重症病例对改善预后至关重要。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 该综述综合了近期在床旁临床体征、常规实验室参数、免疫学标志物以及内皮、肾脏、氧化和代谢功能新兴生物标志物方面的进展,这些均可作为重症肾综合征出血热的早期预警指标。
analysis_zh.current_state: 临床可获取的指标如高热、严重胃肠道症状、精神状态改变、明显出血、血小板减少、白细胞增多以及升高的降钙素原能够可靠预测疾病严重程度,而细胞因子失衡及T细胞和B细胞功能受损则提供了机制性见解。
analysis_zh.gaps: 这些指标的外部验证及其在常规临床实践中的转化仍然缺乏。
analysis_zh.future_research: 未来工作应开发标准化、多中心验证的早期预警系统,以实现对重症肾综合征出血热的精准管理。

papers.title: Andes virus molecular diagnosis and viral RNA kinetics using a research use only RT-PCR assay: Experience from a Spanish tertiary hospital.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the clinical performance and qualitative agreement of a commercially available Research Use Only (RUO) real-time RT-PCR assay for Andes virus (ANDV) detection and longitudinal molecular monitoring during the first imported ANDV outbreak managed in Spain. METHODS: Fourteen repatriated individuals exposed to an ANDV outbreak underwent molecular screening using whole blood and serum specimens. Confirmed cases were prospectively monitored with serial whole blood, serum, oropharyngeal swab, urine, and rectal swab specimens collected every 72 h. Clinical specimens were inactivated in a Biosafety Level 3 facility before automated RNA extraction and testing with the RealStar® Hantavirus-HPS RT-PCR assay (Altona Diagnostics, Hamburg, Germany). All specimens were also analyzed at the Spanish National Reference Laboratory using a hantavirus-specific real-time RT-PCR reference method. Qualitative agreement, Ct value correlation, and viral RNA kinetics were assessed. RESULTS: A total of 185 clinical specimens were analyzed, including 124 screening specimens from exposed individuals and 61 specimens collected during longitudinal follow-up of two confirmed cases. All 124 screening specimens were negative by both assays (124/124, 100% agreement). Among follow-up specimens, overall qualitative agreement was 93.4% (57/61; κ=0.837), and Ct values showed a strong correlation between assays (Pearson's r = 0.965). Four discordant results occurred in specimens with high Ct values (≥34-35), consistent with low concentrations of detectable viral RNA. Whole blood showed the lowest Ct values and the longest persistence of detectable viral RNA among the specimen types evaluated. CONCLUSIONS: The RealStar® Hantavirus-HPS RT-PCR assay showed high qualitative agreement with the reference method in the clinical specimens evaluated and provided timely molecular information during outbreak investigation and longitudinal follow-up. Whole blood may be useful for longitudinal detection of ANDV RNA; however, these findings are descriptive and do not establish generalized viral shedding kinetics or infectivity. Further analytical and clinical studies are required to establish the assay's performance and clinical utility.

source_records.title: Andes virus molecular diagnosis and viral RNA kinetics using a research use only RT-PCR assay: Experience from a Spanish tertiary hospital.
source_records.abstract: Objectives To evaluate the clinical performance and qualitative agreement of a commercially available Research Use Only (RUO) real-time RT-PCR assay for Andes virus (ANDV) detection and longitudinal molecular monitoring during the first imported ANDV outbreak managed in Spain. Methods Fourteen repatriated individuals exposed to an ANDV outbreak underwent molecular screening using whole blood and serum specimens. Confirmed cases were prospectively monitored with serial whole blood, serum, oropharyngeal swab, urine, and rectal swab specimens collected every 72 h. Clinical specimens were inactivated in a Biosafety Level 3 facility before automated RNA extraction and testing with the RealStar® Hantavirus-HPS RT-PCR assay (Altona Diagnostics, Hamburg, Germany). All specimens were also analyzed at the Spanish National Reference Laboratory using a hantavirus-specific real-time RT-PCR reference method. Qualitative agreement, Ct value correlation, and viral RNA kinetics were assessed. Results A total of 185 clinical specimens were analyzed, including 124 screening specimens from exposed individuals and 61 specimens collected during longitudinal follow-up of two confirmed cases. All 124 screening specimens were negative by both assays (124/124, 100% agreement). Among follow-up specimens, overall qualitative agreement was 93.4% (57/61; κ=0.837), and Ct values showed a strong correlation between assays (Pearson's r = 0.965). Four discordant results occurred in specimens with high Ct values (≥34-35), consistent with low concentrations of detectable viral RNA. Whole blood showed the lowest Ct values and the longest persistence of detectable viral RNA among the specimen types evaluated. Conclusions The RealStar® Hantavirus-HPS RT-PCR assay showed high qualitative agreement with the reference method in the clinical specimens evaluated and provided timely molecular information during outbreak investigation and longitudinal follow-up. Whole blood may be useful for longitudinal detection of ANDV RNA; however, these findings are descriptive and do not establish generalized viral shedding kinetics or infectivity. Further analytical and clinical studies are required to establish the assay's performance and clinical utility.

analysis.background: The study aimed to evaluate the clinical performance and qualitative agreement of a commercially available Research Use Only real-time RT‑PCR assay for Andes virus detection and to monitor viral RNA kinetics during the first imported ANDV outbreak managed in Spain.
analysis.methods: Fourteen repatriated individuals exposed to the outbreak were screened using whole blood and serum (A2); confirmed cases were prospectively followed with serial whole blood, serum, oropharyngeal swab, urine, and rectal swab specimens collected every 72 h (A3); specimens were inactivated in a BSL‑3 facility, RNA extracted, and tested with the RealStar® Hantavirus‑HPS RT‑PCR assay (A4); all specimens were also analyzed with a hantavirus‑specific real‑time RT‑PCR reference method (A5); qualitative agreement, Ct value correlation, and viral RNA kinetics were assessed (A6).
analysis.results: A total of 185 clinical specimens were analyzed (124 screening, 61 follow‑up) (A7); all screening specimens were negative by both assays (124/124, 100 % agreement) (A8); follow‑up specimens showed 93.4 % qualitative agreement (57/61, κ=0.837) and strong Ct correlation (Pearson r=0.965) (A9‑A10); four discordant results occurred in specimens with high Ct values (≥34‑35) (A11); whole blood had the lowest Ct values and longest detectable RNA persistence (A12).

analysis.summary_en: Background: The study evaluated a RUO real-time RT‑PCR assay for Andes virus detection and viral RNA kinetics during Spain's first imported ANDV outbreak. Methods: Fourteen repatriated exposed individuals were screened; confirmed cases were followed with serial whole blood, serum, oropharyngeal swab, urine, and rectal swab specimens every 72 h; specimens were inactivated, RNA extracted, and tested with the RealStar® assay alongside a reference RT‑PCR method; qualitative agreement, Ct correlation, and kinetics were assessed. Results: Of 185 specimens (124 screening, 61 follow‑up), screening showed 100 % agreement; follow‑up showed 93.4 % agreement (κ=0.837) and strong Ct correlation (r=0.965); four discordant high‑Ct results occurred; whole blood yielded lowest Ct and longest RNA detection. Contribution: The assay demonstrated high concordance and provided timely molecular data; whole blood appears useful for longitudinal detection, though findings are descriptive. Limitations: Small case number, descriptive nature, no generalized shedding or infectivity data, and only abstract information are available.

papers.title: Hantavirus as a catalyst for urgent One Health preparedness in Africa: strengthening the human-animal-environment interface.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus is a rodent-borne zoonotic pathogen that exposes critical gaps in global and African health preparedness at the human-animal-environment interface. Although historically linked to outbreaks in Asia, Europe, and the Americas, recent events, including a 2026 multi-country Andes virus cluster associated with international travel, underscore its epidemic potential and rare human-to-human transmission. In Africa, no large-scale indigenous outbreaks have been confirmed; however, ecological suitability, weak surveillance systems, and limited diagnostic capacity suggest possible under-detection. This commentary examines global preparedness systems and contrasts them with structural and operational gaps in Africa, including weak laboratory capacity, fragmented surveillance, and limited One Health integration. It also highlights implementation challenges, such as resource constraints and workforce shortages. Beyond technical systems, behavioral and social factors - including risk perception, community engagement, and trust - are essential to effective outbreak response. Strengthening One Health preparedness through laboratory investment, workforce training, regional collaboration, and community-based risk communication is essential to improving resilience against emerging zoonotic diseases.
